fields.m.setting: Separate day school, classroom of 6 with 1:1 staff; nurse on site
fields.m.beh: Head-directed self-injury: striking the head or face with a closed fist or open hand, or hitting the head against a surface, with audible contact. Not: rubbing the eyes, resting the head on the desk.
fields.m.eadesign: multielement with alone and play conditions, 6 series (EA-1, 8/25–9/5); level of differentiation 15%, Subtype 2
fields.m.reinf: Automatic (nonsocial); high across all conditions including alone and play; no social consequence changed it.
fields.m.prec: Rocks faster, hums loudly, brings the hand to the face without contact.
fields.m.repdesc: None; no competing item identified yet.
fields.m.pref: PA-1 (free-operant, 9/8): vibrating pillow, weighted blanket, music with headphones; competing-stimulus assessment scheduled.
fields.m.curr: Instruction is at his level; sessions are short (5 min) with movement breaks.
fields.m.constraints: 1:1 staff; helmet available (padded, prescribed 2025); nurse checks weekly.
fields.m.safety: Bruising and a healed cut over the brow; hits can exceed 20 per minute in bursts; helmet used when a burst starts.
fields.sel.why: From the model's questions; see the rationale on each card.
fields.cp[0].s0: For items that did not compete in the standard assessment, add prompted engagement (physical or model prompts to interact with the item) during the session.
fields.cp[0].s1: Add response blocking of the target behavior during item sessions so engagement can contact the item's stimulation.
fields.cp[0].s2: Fade prompts and blocking while measuring whether reduction holds; items that hold are carried into treatment.
fields.cp[0].s3: Re-run the standard assessment periodically to confirm the items still compete.
fields.cp[1].s0: Define the interruption: on each occurrence, gain attention and present 2–3 demands for an incompatible response (vocal for vocal stereotypy; motor for motor stereotypy) until the student complies without the target.
fields.cp[1].s1: Praise compliance; return to the ongoing activity.
fields.cp[1].s2: For dangerous topographies, block neutrally per the safety plan.
fields.cp[1].s3: Combine with matched stimulation and DRA so appropriate behavior is reinforced.
fields.cp[1].s4: Record occurrences, interruptions delivered, and appropriate responses.
fields.cp[2].s0: Report the functional-analysis pattern, subtype, and LOD to the prescriber and nurse; request evaluation for pain, illness, or other medical contributors.
fields.cp[2].s1: Track any medication and its side effects on Form MS-1 and share the behavioral data at each review.
fields.cp[2].s2: Keep protective and behavioral components in place while medical questions are pursued; no medication decisions are made on this form.
fields.cp[3].s0: Obtain medical clearance for the protective equipment and apply it throughout the re-test; hold it constant across conditions.
fields.cp[3].s1: Begin each block with consecutive alone sessions under the equipment until the behavior decreases (automatic extinction).
fields.cp[3].s2: Then run consecutive attention or play sessions (attention test) and, in separate blocks, demand or play sessions (escape test), selected by a random schedule.
fields.cp[3].s3: Interpret elevated responding in a test condition relative to play as a social function; treat it with the matched component and withhold that consequence.
fields.cp[3].s4: Do not use the equipment alone as treatment while social consequences still follow the behavior.
fields.cp[4].s0: Specify protective equipment, blocking rules, and staffing for sessions and the school day.
fields.cp[4].s1: Obtain medical clearance and a nursing review schedule.
fields.cp[4].s2: Define crisis-response steps separate from the treatment procedure so they are not delivered as consequences that could reinforce behavior.
fields.cp[5].s0: Provide a visual or picture activity schedule the student manipulates (check off, move a card) as each activity ends.
fields.cp[5].s1: Give an advance notice before transitions (e.g., 2-min and 30-s warnings) and a consistent transition signal.
fields.cp[5].s2: Preview any change to the routine at the start of the day; keep the order stable where possible.
fields.cp[5].s3: For transition-evoked behavior, combine with the function-based component identified on EA-1 (Wilder et al., 2006).
fields.cp[6].s0: Preview the next day's or next period's materials in a low-demand, preferred context (with a parent or aide) before the lesson.
fields.cp[6].s1: Keep priming brief and reinforcing; do not test.
fields.cp[6].s2: Track performance and problem behavior in the primed lessons versus unprimed ones.
fields.cp[7].s0: At arrival, check the setting events the assessment identified (sleep, illness, allergy symptoms, missed medication, conflict on the bus or at home, hunger) with the parent note or a brief check.
fields.cp[7].s1: When a setting event is present, run the neutralizing routine: a preferred activity first, reduced or shortened demands, extra noncontingent attention, and choice for that morning (Horner et al., 1997).
fields.cp[7].s2: Record the setting event and the routine used on the data sheet; report medical setting events to the nurse.
fields.cp[8].s0: Schedule vigorous aerobic activity (e.g., jogging, stationary bike, trampoline) before the periods with the most problem behavior or stereotypy; mild activity did not produce the effect (Kern et al., 1984).
fields.cp[8].s1: Set the duration individually: continue until a behavioral indicator of satiation (e.g., the student stops or slows) rather than a fixed clock time (Neely et al., 2015); obtain medical clearance.
fields.cp[8].s2: Measure the behavior in the window after exercise to confirm the effect and its duration; adjust placement in the schedule.
fields.cp[8].s3: Pair with instruction that follows immediately.
fields.cp[9].s0: Assess preference with the method chosen in part B; separate leisure from edible classes.
fields.cp[9].s1: Set access duration to match the treatment context (Steinhilber & Johnson, 2007); use accumulated access for activities that lose value when interrupted.
fields.cp[9].s2: Validate with a reinforcer assessment; rotate items and offer choice.
fields.cp[10].s0: Completing a unit schedule (e.g., FR 3 correct) earns a token; completing the exchange schedule (e.g., 5 tokens) earns the backup reinforcer.
fields.cp[10].s1: Establish tokens by pairing with immediate exchange at first (exchange after 1 token), then lengthen the exchange requirement.
fields.cp[10].s2: Offer a menu of backup reinforcers to limit satiation; keep the exchange schedule dense enough to contact the backup daily.
fields.cp[10].s3: Thin the unit schedule before the exchange schedule.
fields.cp[11].s0: Line up 5–7 items; the student approaches one and receives brief access; remove it and re-present the rest until all are chosen or 30 s passes without a choice.
fields.cp[11].s1: Repeat 3–5 times; rank by mean selection order or percentage.
fields.cp[11].s2: Use the brief version before sessions to track daily shifts (DeLeon et al., 2001).
fields.cp[12].s0: Reinforce a response only if it follows the previous one by at least the set interresponse time (spaced-responding DRL), or reinforce at the end of a period in which the count stayed at or below a criterion (full-session DRL).
fields.cp[12].s1: Set the initial criterion from baseline so reinforcement is contacted on most opportunities.
fields.cp[12].s2: Lower the allowed rate in steps toward the goal; the goal is a reduced, not zero, rate.
fields.cp[13].s0: Begin with the prompt that guarantees the response (e.g., full physical), delivered immediately with the instruction.
fields.cp[13].s1: Reduce to the next less intrusive level after the criterion (e.g., 3 consecutive correct); return one level after 2 errors.
fields.cp[13].s2: Reinforce prompted responses during acquisition; differentially reinforce unprompted responses once they appear.
fields.cp[13].s3: Use when errors evoke problem behavior or the response is new.
fields.cp[14].s0: Begin with a 0-s delay between instruction and prompt; increase the delay in small steps (e.g., 1 s per session or per criterion) as unprompted responses appear.
fields.cp[14].s1: Transfer of control is shown when the learner responds before the prompt; keep the terminal delay short enough to prevent errors.
fields.cp[14].s2: Reinforce unprompted responses more richly than prompted ones.
fields.cp[15].s0: Compare candidate prompt types (vocal, model, physical) or hierarchies (MTL vs LTM) on equivalent skill sets in an alternating-treatments design.
fields.cp[15].s1: Select the procedure that produced the fastest acquisition with the fewest errors and least problem behavior.
fields.cp[15].s2: Re-run when a new response class is introduced.
fields.cp[16].s0: After an error, model or deliver the correct response, then re-present the instruction and require an independent (or least-prompted) correct response before moving on.
fields.cp[16].s1: Reinforce the corrected response with praise only; reserve the token or item for unprompted responses.
fields.cp[17].s0: Offer the student a choice at session start between the treatment area, a hangout area with free reinforcers, and leaving; honor the choice without programmed consequences.
fields.cp[17].s1: Run skill-based treatment only when the student opts in; make the treatment area richer over time so opting in increases.
fields.cp[17].s2: Record choices and problem behavior in each area; use for students with restraint or escalation histories.
fields.cp[18].s0: Identify the reinforcer and the establishing operation that makes it valuable (deprivation, an interrupted chain, a missing item).
fields.cp[18].s1: Contrive the EO (interrupt a chain by withholding a needed item; present the preferred item and remove it) and wait briefly for the mand.
fields.cp[18].s2: Prompt the mand form (vocal, sign, picture, device) and deliver the specific reinforcer immediately; fade prompts with a progressive delay so the EO, not the prompt, controls the mand (Sweeney-Kerwin et al., 2007).
fields.cp[18].s3: Run many trials per session across items; record prompted and unprompted mands.
fields.cp[19].s0: Capture naturally occurring EOs during routines (snack, play, transitions); pause and wait for the mand before providing the item or action.
fields.cp[19].s1: Prompt only as needed, fade quickly, and reinforce with the item requested.
fields.cp[19].s2: Rotate across settings, listeners, and items to build generalized manding; record mands per hour in the natural routine.
fields.cp[20].s0: Assess the must-have skills first: requesting, waiting after requests, accepting removals and transitions, completing brief tasks, accepting "no," and health and safety routines.
fields.cp[20].s1: Select the alternative method of speaking (vocal, sign, picture, device) from the student's repertoire and teach requests first.
fields.cp[20].s2: Sequence the remaining must-have skills alongside the reduction plan; record the level of prompting and the settings in which each skill occurs.
fields.cp[21].p2: CR-1: a burst over 5 minutes or any bleeding: nurse, parent call, the second adult.
fields.cp[21].s0: On the precursor: At faster rocking or the hand to the face: offer the vibrating pillow and headphones (competing items), move to the padded area, start the 1-minute check.
fields.cp[21].s1: On the target behavior: Block the strike with a cushion; put the helmet on at the second strike of a burst (prescribed); keep speech neutral; present a competing item every 30 s.
fields.cp[21].s2: After the episode: Nurse check for any mark; record the burst length and the items used on DD-1; helmet off after 2 minutes without a strike.
fields.cp[21].s3: Staff do not: Do not hold his arms; do not reprimand; do not remove demands as a consequence (no social function).
fields.cp[21].s4: Record the episode, the step used, and whether the reinforcer was contacted (integrity error).
fields.cp[21].s5: Crisis procedure applies only when the safety trigger is met and is documented separately.
fields.cp[22].bsrc: Preferred toys, brief hand redirection and praise check-ins for automatically maintained hair pulling (Vorndran et al., 2008)
fields.cp[22].p0: the three top items from a paired-stimulus preference assessment (button-press sound book, baby doll, small purse); later, novel toys with lights, sounds or spinning parts chosen through a single-stimulus assessment
fields.cp[22].p1: toys continuously within reach; staff check-ins began every 30 s and were lengthened by 15 to 30 s after 2 consecutive sessions with hair pulling at least 75% below the baseline mean, reaching 300 s in the classroom
fields.cp[22].p2: the authors recommend daily preference checks; new toys were added when hair pulling rose as check-ins were stretched past 180 to 210 s
fields.cp[22].s0: Run a paired-stimulus preference assessment and place the three most preferred toys within the student's reach during independent play.
fields.cp[22].s1: Set a timer for check-ins, starting at every 30 s.
fields.cp[22].s2: At a check-in, if the student is pulling hair, gently guide one hand to the lap and place a toy in the other hand without any other comment or attention.
fields.cp[22].s3: At a check-in, if the student is not pulling hair, give brief praise, make sure all toys are within reach, and remind the student that the toys are there.
fields.cp[22].s4: Leave after the brief interaction and wait for the next check-in; give no consequence for thumb sucking.
fields.cp[22].s5: After 2 consecutive sessions with hair pulling at least 75% below the baseline mean, lengthen the check-in interval by 15 to 30 s, working toward 300 s.
fields.cp[22].s6: If hair pulling rises or toy play drops after a lengthening, go back to the last successful interval (the study moved from 210 s to 180 s) and add novel toys with light, sound or spinning features.
fields.cp[22].s7: After the plan works in a controlled setting, train classroom staff by modeling it and then coaching them while they run it, with periodic integrity checks.
fields.cp[22].data: Percentage of 10-s intervals with hair pulling and with thumb sucking in 10-min sessions (partial-interval recording), the current check-in interval, and notes on toy engagement.
fields.cp[22].mat: Highly preferred toys from the preference assessment, novel toys with light, sound or spinning features, a timer or silent cue for check-ins, a play area with a beanbag chair, interval data sheet.
fields.cp[23].bsrc: Protective mittens faded to cut-down gloves for automatically reinforced eye pressing (Luiselli, 1991)
fields.cp[23].p0: touch and light sensations from finger-to-eye contact; eye pressing was far lower when padded mittens blocked contact (14.8 vs 33.5 per hour)
fields.cp[23].p1: large padded mittens with wrist straps, then tight batting gloves, then latex gloves, then the latex glove cut down in 4 steps (rolled to the base of the hand, rolled to the base of the thumb, fingers 3–5 cut off, thumb and index cut off) before removal
fields.cp[23].p2: eye exams ruled out raised eye pressure and infection; medical staff worried about tissue damage and bleeding; the facility review committee and the parents approved the program
fields.cp[23].s0: Have the nurse and doctor rule out eye pressure, infection and other medical causes before starting.
fields.cp[23].s1: Run brief comparisons of coverings on and off to confirm that blocking finger-to-eye contact lowers the behavior.
fields.cp[23].s2: Put the protective covering on for the school day and keep preferred switch toys and activities on the student's tray.
fields.cp[23].s3: Each time the student touches an eye, gently guide the hand back to the lap tray without comment.
fields.cp[23].s4: When rates stay low, switch to a thinner covering in the order mittens, batting gloves, latex gloves.
fields.cp[23].s5: Cut the latex glove down in steps: roll it to the base of the hand, then to the base of the thumb, then cut off three fingers, then the thumb and index finger.
fields.cp[23].s6: If eye pressing rises after a step, go back to the previous step and stay there longer before trying again.
fields.cp[23].s7: Remove the last piece of glove and keep counting eye pressing every hour.
fields.cp[23].data: Eye presses counted per hour with a tally counter during 3 morning hours each day and entered on a data sheet.
fields.cp[23].mat: Padded mittens with wrist straps, batting gloves, latex gloves cut down by step, lap tray with switch toys, tally counter.
fields.cp[24].bsrc: Immediate response interruption for automatically maintained skin picking or hair twirling (Kliebert et al., 2011)
fields.cp[24].p1: interrupt every attempt at once (0-s delay) at the first movement toward skin, clothing or another person's hair, guiding the hands to the lap for about 1 s; apply it in every setting where the behavior occurs
fields.cp[24].p2: none programmed; highly preferred leisure items were freely available for one learner but did not compete with the behavior
fields.cp[24].s0: Assign one staff member to sit directly beside the student, within arm's reach, for the whole period the plan covers.
fields.cp[24].s1: Watch the student's hands continuously and take on no other tasks while the procedure is in effect.
fields.cp[24].s2: At the first movement toward picking (fingers to skin or clothing) or toward someone's hair, block it immediately, with no delay.
fields.cp[24].s3: Guide the student's hands to the lap for about 1 s, then let go.
fields.cp[24].s4: Resume the ongoing activity without comment or any other consequence.
fields.cp[24].s5: Stay close enough to reach every attempt at once; do not plan to walk over after the behavior has started.
fields.cp[24].s6: Use the same procedure in every room and activity where the behavior occurs, because the effect did not transfer to untreated settings.
fields.cp[24].s7: After any session in which picking causes bleeding, clean the wound and give first aid as the school nurse directs.
fields.cp[24].s8: Record attempts per minute, counting blocked attempts, and note any delay before interruption.
fields.cp[24].data: Attempts per minute (skin picks or hair twirls, including blocked attempts) in 10-min sessions, with the delay before each interruption noted; compare treated and untreated settings.
fields.cp[24].mat: Preferred leisure items identified by caregiver or teacher interview and a paired-item preference assessment; first-aid supplies for open wounds.
fields.sch.0: reducing a rate without eliminating the behavior
fields.sch.1: no, time is easier to track
fields.ec.0: no, the prompting procedure is errorless
fields.rb.prec: At faster rocking or the hand to the face: offer the vibrating pillow and headphones (competing items), move to the padded area, start the 1-minute check.
fields.rb.target: Block the strike with a cushion; put the helmet on at the second strike of a burst (prescribed); keep speech neutral; present a competing item every 30 s.
fields.rb.after: Nurse check for any mark; record the burst length and the items used on DD-1; helmet off after 2 minutes without a strike.
fields.rb.not: Do not hold his arms; do not reprimand; do not remove demands as a consequence (no social function).
fields.rb.crisis: CR-1: a burst over 5 minutes or any bleeding: nurse, parent call, the second adult.
fields.p.visit: Weekly 30-minute visit: observe one session, score the integrity checklist, give feedback, model any step under 80%.
fields.p.pre: Probes before the plan starts: the target and the replacement behavior in 3 settings (class, specials, cafeteria) with 2 adults.
fields.p.gen: Train with two adults and in two settings from the first week; the natural cue (the demand itself) is the SD; the card goes with the student.
fields.p.post: Probes in the untrained setting at 2 and 4 weeks after criterion; monthly after.
fields.p.complex: The simple response first; the longer form once the simple one is at criterion.
fields.p.design: Baseline to treatment with the EA-1 treatment sheet; reversal only if the team agrees.
